summary: בכר is being first: the firstborn son or daughter, the first male of the herd and flock, the fruit that ripens first, and the firstborn's standing and double share (בְּכֹרָה). Scripture sets the firstborn beside “the beginning (רֵאשִׁית) of strength” (Gen 49:3; Deu 21:17). Every firstborn in Israel belongs to Yahweh, who calls Israel “my son, my firstborn” (Exo 4:22); and the first-ripe fruits, בִּכּוּרִים, are brought to his house, the loaves of the feast of weeks among them (Lev 23:17, 20). The New Testament calls Christ the firstborn of the dead. Arabic بِكْر and باكورة, Akkadian bukru, Ugaritic and Punic bkr share the meaning; Arabic and Akkadian also name a young camel or foal from the root.

doctrine.statement: Yahweh sent Moses to say to Pharaoh, “Israel is my son, my firstborn: let my son go… if you refuse, I will kill your son, your firstborn” (Exo 4:22–23). On the night he struck every firstborn in Egypt, the firstborn of Israel were spared (Exo 12:12–13), and from that day every firstborn in Israel, of man and beast, was his: “on the day I struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I set apart for myself every firstborn in Israel” (Num 3:13; Exo 13:2). The firstborn sons were to be redeemed (Exo 13:13, 15), and the Levites were taken for Yahweh in their place (Num 3:12). Hebrews reads the keeping of the פֶּסַח as faith, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them (Heb 11:28). Mary's firstborn son was presented in the temple, as the law of the Lord says, “every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luk 2:7, 22–23, from Exo 13:2, 12). The firstborn live because Yahweh spared them, and so they are his.

Of David's heir Yahweh says, “He will call to me, ‘You are my Father’… and I will make him firstborn, highest of the kings of the earth” (Psa 89:27–28). John calls Jesus “the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Rev 1:5). Scripture calls the firstborn “the beginning (רֵאשִׁית) of his strength” (Gen 49:3; Deu 21:17), and Paul joins the same two words of Christ: “he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he may be first” (Col 1:18), as he is “the firstborn of all creation” (Col 1:15). He is the firstborn among many brothers, conformed to his image (Rom 8:29), and those who come to God come to “the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven” (Heb 12:23). Zechariah foretold mourning over the one they pierced “as one mourns over a firstborn” (Zec 12:10), and John cites that verse at the cross (Jhn 19:37).

The birthright went with birth, not with a father's favour: he may not make the son of the loved wife firstborn over the son of the hated, but must give the firstborn a double portion (Deu 21:15–17). Esau sold his for a meal of bread and lentils and despised it (Gen 25:31–34), and later lost the blessing too (Gen 27:36). Reuben lost his by defiling his father's bed, and it went to the sons of Joseph (1Ch 5:1–2). Hebrews warns that no one be godless like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright and afterward, wanting the blessing, was rejected, though he sought it with tears (Heb 12:16–17).

note: Left out: the names בִּכְרִי (Bichri), בֶּכֶר (Becher, b.br.ac), בַּכְרִי (Becherite), בֹּכְרוּ (Bocheru), בְּכוֹרַת (Becorath); and בַּלְאֲדָן (Baladan, b.br.ao), an Akkadian royal name filed here by BDB, not formed from this root. בֶּכֶר “young camel” has no BDB key of its own: its one token (Isa 60:6) is counted under b.br.ag with בִּכְרָה. Firstfruits in the New Testament: “Christ the firstfruits (ἀπαρχή) of those who sleep” (1Co 15:20–23), and ἀπαρχή in Jas 1:18 and Rev 14:4, answer to רֵאשִׁית, not to בִּכּוּרִים: the Peshitta renders all three with רִשִׁיתָא, and the sheaf brought on the morrow after the sabbath is the רֵאשִׁית of the harvest (Lev 23:10), while בִּכּוּרִים are the loaves of the fiftieth day (Lev 23:17, 20). Those passages belong in the doctrine of a ראשׁ entry, so no firstfruits doctrine is written here. Open: (1) Should a doctrine note that the day of the בִּכּוּרִים (Num 28:26) is the fiftieth day (Lev 23:16), the day on which Luke dates the coming of the Spirit (Act 2:1)? Scripture states both facts but does not connect the Spirit with the בִּכּוּרִים loaves, so it is left for review. (2) Ge'ez bakwara, which Anderson–Moser gloss “offer” (GEZ001030), not checked in Dillmann or Leslau; not entered. (3) Ugaritic and Punic bkr from Anderson–Moser only; Akkadian bukru “son” not checked in CAD for “firstborn heir”. (4) The young-camel words: Arabic and Akkadian share them, but scripture's use does not show the tie to “first”; Lane's بَكْر is a camel in its youth, which may be the link (the first years). Similar-sounding root: בקר (qof for kaph) gives בֹּקֶר “morning”, while Arabic بَكَرَ / بُكْرَة (this root) is “go early in the morning; early morning”. The two Hebrew roots differ only in k/q, both stops at the back of the mouth; noted for cross-root work (see the baqar entry), not as evidence that they are one root.
